newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia dlr ekes out rare firmer close for week.
newsitem.headline: Australia dlr ekes out rare firmer close for week.

text.p: The Australian dollar bounced from key support on Friday, the first time in almost two months it had ended a week higher than it began, if only modestly.

A pause in the downtrend was not unexpected, given it had fallen 6.25 percent since peaking at 80 cents in mid-March and dealers suspected the market was short enough to allow a test of US$0.7530 near term and even a push to US$0.7570.

However, no one was going to get carried away while there remained a real possibility of the Reserve Bank cutting domestic interest rates for a fifth time, a risk most analysts rated at more than 50 percent for July.
By 5.00 pm (0700 GMT) the local currency was hovering at US$0.7511/16, up on Thursday's US$0.7475/80 finish and a whisker above the US$0.7507 level seen last Friday.
The overnight session, like the week, was characterised by a vigorous two-way tussle between speculators vying to trigger stop loss orders either side of US$0.7470 and US$0.7530.
Neither attempt has won so far, although traders tend to favour a break lower and have targets of US$0.7450, US$0.7420 and US$0.7380 in mind before an eventual goal of 73 cents.
A push above the US$0.7630/80 resistance band was needed to reverse the downtrend.
Dealers reckoned such a recovery a distant possibility given the market remained on alert for a Reserve Bank rate cut following a run of dire economic data in recent weeks.

The 90-day bank bill contract for September, a good guide to market thinking on rates, had settled at 94.86 which implied a rate of 5.14 percent compared to the present official level of 5.50 percent. This was some way below the IMM three month Eurodollar contract which stood at 94.135, implying the market expected a hike from the present 5.50 percent Fed funds rate.
This was the crux of the A$'s problems since it was almost unprecedented for rates here to be under those in the U.S.
This was not exactly unjustified given Australia and the US were on different stages of the economic cycle and inflation had averaged less than the U.S. for most of the 1990's.
Indeed, the last RBA rate cut on May 23 promised to see headline inflation growth slow even further from its 1.5 percent level recorded in the March quarter.

A Reuter survey of 27 economists found the majority expected the CPI measure to fall to around 0.7 percent in Q2 and Q3, while underlying inflation was seen easing to around 1.7 percent from 2.1 percent in Q1. The RBA's mandate is to keep underlying inflation in a 2-3 percent band over the life of a cycle.
On the crosses it recouped a little lost ground on the yen to 85.94/04 from 84.90/00 late yesterday.
It benefited from a bounce in US$/yen which saw the U.S. dollar add a yen to 114.50 following a lower than expected U.S. trade deficit for April.
In trade weighted terms the local unit edged up to 57.1 from a previous 56.8 close.

There were no domestic data out today and the next official release is May quarter job vacancies on Thursday and new motor vehicle registrations for May on Friday, neither of which is likely to set the market on fire. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
